content.title: Recap: A record-setting day at the Boston Marathon
content.text: Monday is the 130th Boston Marathon, the world's oldest and most prestigious annual marathon. More than 30,000 runners from around the world are competing in the 26.2-mile race from Hopkinton to Copley Square.Kenya's John Korir won his second straight Boston Marathon in the men's division, finishing at 2:01:52 and setting a new course record. Fellow Kenyan Sharon Lokedi, the defending women's winner, also repeated as champion with a time of 2:18:51. Marcel Hug of Switzerland, nicknamed "The Silver Bullet," won his ninth Boston Marathon in the men's wheelchair division, with a time of 1:16:06, missing his own course record by 33 seconds. He is now just one win short of Ernst Van Dyk's all-category record of 10. Eden Rainbow-Cooper of Britain won the women's wheelchair division, her second Boston win, in 1:30:51. Every year, a small subset of marathon runners ups the ante by not just running 26.2 miles in one go, but doing it in costume. Here are some of those bold athletes. Greg Derr/USA Today Network / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn ImagesA runner dressed in banana suit during the 130th running of the Boston Marathon at Heartbreak Hill. Greg Derr/USA Today Network / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn ImagesA runner dressed like he's taking a shower crests Heartbreak Hill during the 130th running of the Boston Marathon. Daily News and Wicked Local Staff Photo/Art Illman / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn ImagesFrom left: Reid Fuhr, Aaron Grushow, Jason Britt, Wingdham Woods, and Joshua Cote, all dressed as former U.S. men's national soccer team star Alexi Lalas, await their start at the 130th running of the Boston Marathon. Spectators cheered on runners as they neared the finish line Monday. The BAA released the finish times of some of the notable participants in Monday's edition of the marathon: Des Linden, 2018 Boston Marathon champion – 2:36:24 Former Boston Bruins captain Zdeno Chara – 3:18:13 Jeff DaRosa of the Dropkick Murphys – 3:44:10 Chelsea Clinton – 3:48:12 Running comedian Laura Green – 3:52:21 Bryan Arenales, winner of "Love Island" season 7 – 4:17:35 Amby Burfoot, 1968 Boston Marathon champion – 5:17:16 Former Boston Celtics player Chris Herren – 5:17:23 Former U.S. women's national team star Kristine Lilly (Heavey) – 5:22:02 Retired astronaut Suni Williams – 5:53:36 A Nike sign that read, "Runners welcome. Walkers tolerated," was pulled down amid backlash. Nike put up a new sign and shared a statement about the matter. An NBC10 Boston viewer who lives in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia came to say hi at the marathon finish line and shared her connection to a former champion from 100 years ago. Tanya Brann-Barrett was running in honor of Johnny Miles, who won both the 1926 and 1929 races. The Cape Breton Islander stunned the field with his first win, which made him an instant celebrity in Boston, according to his obituary in The New York Times. NBC10 BostonTanya Brann-Barrett at the finish line of the 2026 Boston Marathon. Boston and Nova Scotia have a decadeslong bond forged in the deadly Halifax explosion of 1917, which was the largest man-made blast until the start of the nuclear age. Doctors and nurses rushed north from Boston to help; as a thank you, Nova Scotia has been sending a huge Christmas tree to Boston each year. When a massive explosion rocked the Canadian city of Halifax in December 1917, creating the world's first mushroom cloud and killing thousands, hundreds of medical workers from Massachusetts raced through a blizzard to help. The kindness led to the annual gift of a Nova Scotian Christmas tree for Boston. We've been following the retired astronaut's plans for running on Patriots' Day pretty closely. Watch Jeff Saperstone's interview with her last week here: Sunita Williams says she is excited to run the Boston Marathon, noting preparing for it has had its good days and bad days. Plus, she shares the first thing she might do after crossing the finish line. Suni Williams has run the Boston Marathon before, but this time she did it on Earth. When the Needham native ran the Boston Marathon while aboard the space station back in 2007, she was the first person to complete a 26.2-mile run in space, doing it with an unofficial time of 4:23:46. Almost 20 years later, and feeling the effects of Earth's gravity with every step, the recently retired astronaut famous for her marathon stay in space in 2024-2025, finished the marathon in 5:52:49. More on Suni Williams' Boston Marathons Zouhair Talbi and Jess McClain ran the fastest times ever for Americans at the Boston Marathon on Monday, both finishing fifth in their respective divisions. Talbi finished in 2 hours, 3 minutes, 45 seconds in the men's race. McClain finished in 2:20:49 in the women's competition. There were seven American men and 12 American women in the top 20, including five women in the top 10. “I think we’re in an era in distance running, on the men and women’s sides, but especially the women’s side, where we’re all making each other so much better every time we line up with one another,” McClain said. “And I think it’s just going to get stronger and stronger.” BOSTON, MA - April 20: Jess McClain celebrates finishing the 130th Boston Marathon on April 20, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Rinaldi/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) That's what's it's going to take, Talbi said, to take American distance running to the next level. Jaiden Tripi/Getty ImagesBill and Hillary Clinton are seen with daughter Chelsea Clinton after she finished the 130th Boston Marathon on Monday, April 20, 2026. Chelsea Clinton was one of the celebrities who ran the Boston Marathon on Monday, though she was probably the only one with a former president and secretary of state waiting to congratulate her when she crossed the finish line. Bill and Hillary Clinton celebrated with their daughter, an author, podcaster and public health advocate. How fast did Clinton cross the finish line? A search of her name on the marathon's results page didn't return anything, but her bib number did: Margaret Smith, who was listed as being, like Clinton, a New Yorker between 45 and 49. She finished in 3:40:52 — an 8:26-mile pace. Clinton has written about a famous Margaret Smith before: trailblazing member of Congress Margaret Chase Smith, who represented Maine in the U.S. House and Senate and was the first woman to serve in both. She was also the first woman to actively seek a major political party's nomination for president. Read Full ArticleA Nike sign that read, “Runners welcome. Walkers tolerated,” was pulled down amid backlash. Nike put up a new sign and shared a statement about the matter. Marathon Monday really celebrates the determination and resilience of every runner who crosses that finish line. But just steps away from Boylston Street, a controversial ad from Nike is drawing attention after many say it sent the wrong message about who belongs in the race. This is one of the most inspiring days in Boston, when elite athletes and everyday runners share the same course. But in the week leading up to the marathon, a sign here at the Nike store had some people questioning that spirit. Right near the finish line of the Boston Marathon, a message meant to motivate runners instead sparked backlash. The sign, displayed at Nike's Newbury Street store, read "RUNNERS WELCOME. WALKERS TOLERATED." Online critics called it dismissive, and many found it to be at odds with the spirit of the marathon. Read Full Article Chelsea Clinton mingled with her parents, former President Bill and former Secretary of State Hilary, after finishing in 3:40:52 Running comedian Laura Green finished in 03:50:17. The elite runners can sometimes make the Boston Marathon look easy, but the truth is... it's a lot. And runners are often overwhelmed by emotion, exhaustion or both as they cross the finish line. Here's a look at some amazing images from the finish line so far this year. A runner celebrates after crossing the finish line during the 130th Boston Marathon in Boston, Massachusetts, on April 20, 2026. (Photo by Joseph Prezioso / AFP via Getty Images) Runners cross the finish line during the 130th Boston Marathon in Boston, Massachusetts, on April 20, 2026. (Photo by Joseph Prezioso / AFP via Getty Images) A runner is helped after crossing the finish line during the 130th Boston Marathon in Boston, Massachusetts, on April 20, 2026. (Photo by Joseph Prezioso / AFP via Getty Images) Runners cross the finish line during the 130th Boston Marathon in Boston, Massachusetts, on April 20, 2026. (Photo by Joseph Prezioso / AFP via Getty Images) Gov. Maura Healey's takeaway from Marathon Monday was mainly gratitude for everyone who makes it possible, she said. "It's just a day you can't help but feel anything but great about," Healey said. Looking ahead to the many events being hosted in and around Boston this summer, she wouldn't pick a favorite, but did note how great it will be to have the Boston Pops playing on the Charles River Esplanade on this July 4, the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. And Healey said Massachusetts is ready to hos it all. "People have been working hard planning for all these different events. It's a lot at once but here in Boston we're used to major events," she said, adding she's thankful for all those working behind the scenes planning those events, too. Wearing bib number 3333, the former Bruins captain finished the race in 3:18:13, a pace of just over 7:30 minutes/mile. Chara, who now works in the B's front office, has been running the race for several years. Of the Bruins' third-period collapse in their opening 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, Chara said, "We're gonna bounce back." Mayor Michelle Wu said that watching the marathon is great because, "This is a time in the world where it feels like we need good news." She noted that Marathon Monday is also Patriots' Day in Boston, where "we also commemorate Boston's role in running that race to a more perfect union." Looking ahead to the city's plans for America 250, the celebrations of the country's semiquincentennial anniversary, and other big events in Boston, Wu said, "We are ready to go." "This is the time for everyone to see Boston, what we represent, how we come together, and it's going to be an amazing, fun, welcoming time," she added. Linden, the last American to win the Boston Marathon, was back on the course Monday, wearing the year of her victory as her bib number. Linden didn't win — she was the 30th-fastest woman this year — but her goal was really having fun. She ran the race with her husband. Nevertheless, she actually bested her 2018 time of 2:39:54, finishing this year with 2:35:49. But conditions were more favorable this year, and she said of the top women and their times, "Mind blown, incredible day." People have been surprised that she'd come back, Linden said, but she made it seem like a no-brainer: "It's a treat in the spring!" Legends in their sports — Pedro Martinez, Tedy Bruschi, Clint Dempsey and Des Linden — taught the fundamentals to students at the Curley school in Jamaica Plain. Lokedi went into more detail on what she was thinking as dashed to a repeat victory. When she was in front, she thought, "I'm not going to look back, I'm just going to follow the lead car." She said she felt like she was going faster than she had the year before, but, "I didn't know how fast I was running or how fast I was going." Instead, she thought, "This is good rhythm, I'll just stick with it for as long as I can." After his back-to-back victories, Korir was asked if he might come back to go for the three-peat in 2027. The Kenyan didn't commit either way, saying it was in the hands of his manager: "If my manager say(s), hey, we are going back to Boston, i'll go back." Never run the Boston Marathon? Here's what all the competitors get to see after they finish the 26.2 miles. After her big win, Lokedi gave a lot of credit to the love she felt from the crowd. "Everybody is cheering for me and it felt so good," she said. She repeated to herself to be patient and humble, she said, and then got a boost from a girl she heard along the course who yelled out, "You got this, ladies!" "It was so cute. That was what I needed," Lokedi said. She came in fifth place overall, with a time of 2:20:49. "I'm very honored that it went this way for me this year … you have to celebrate every finish line for sure," she said after crossing the finish line. Sharon Lokedi of Kenya just took first place in the women's division of the 2026 Boston Marathon — for the second year in a row. Her 2025 marathon remains the record for fastest time a woman has run the Boston Marathon. "I had no problems from the start to the finish," Korir said. Korir beat his time from last year by almost three minutes, breaking the all-time record for the Boston Marathon. The previous record dates back to 2011. "I enjoyed," he said. Reigning women's champion Sharon Lokedi of Kenya is one of three women leading the Boston Marathon field with five miles left. Lokedi is in first, trailed by Loice Chemnung and Irine Cheptai, also of Kenya. John Korir of Kenya won the Boston Marathon in the men's professional division — for the second year in a row. Korir won Boston in 2025, and won Chicago in 2024. His 2026 Boston time was 2:01:52 — the fastest ever in the marathon's history. Marcel Hug and Eden Rainbow-Cooper hold the trophy after finishing in first place in the men's and women's wheelchair divisions during the 130th Boston Marathon. It was Hug's ninth Boston win and Rainbow-Cooper's second. Getty Images(L/R) Marcel Hug and Eden Rainbow-Cooper hold the trophy after finishing in first place in the men's and women's wheelchair divisions during the 130th Boston Marathon on April 20, 2026, in Boston, Massachusetts. (Photo by Joseph Prezioso / AFP via Getty Images) John Korir has just taken the lead in the men's professional field at the 20 mile mark of the 2026 Boston Marathon. He passed Ethiopian runner Milkesa Mengesha. Korir's, the reigning men's champion, finished in 2:04:45 last year, the third-fastest time ever as he joined his brother to become a Boston Marathon champion. Rainbow-Cooper said it was "amazing" to win another Boston. "The only way is up so it means a lot to me," she said. She said there's a lot of people who don't have the opportunity to do what she does, and she was doing the race for them, too. "It [Boston] feels like home," the Britain native said. Hopkinton, MA - April 20: Runners start the 130th Boston Marathon on April 20, 2026. (Photo by David L. Ryan/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) See our full photo gallery from the 130th Boston Marathon here NBC10 BostonVolunteers check over the medals that will be awarded to runners who cross the finish line of the 130th Boston Marathon Eden Rainbow-Cooper of Britain has won the women's wheelchair division. She previously won the Boston Marathon in 2024. Hug just gave an interview after winning his ninth Boston. He says it never gets old. "Such a fantastic race," he said. "I felt good from the beginning." "I was impressed I was already alone after the downhill," he added. Hug said he was trying to break the course record, but lost some time in the second half. Marcel Hug was the first in the men's wheelchair division to cross the finish line, marking his ninth victory at the Boston Marathon. He finished the course with a time of 1:16:05. The professional women have started their marathon and are officially making their way through the course. Sharon Lokedi of Kenya is the defending champion, and is going for the top spot once again this year. American women runners to watch include Emily Sisson, Sara Hall and Susanna Sullivan. Bruins great Zdeno Chara, a marathon finisher himself, served as the honorary starter at Monday's Boston Marathon, firing the starting gun for the men's professional division. He's also running the race later in the day. Des Linden, who is also running, fired the starting gun for the women's professional division. NBC10 BostonThe finish line at the 130th Boston Marathon Several waves of runners have taken off from Hopkinton, but things are quiet on Boylston Street for now. Here's a quick look at the scene inside the Boston Marathon media room on Monday morning as the race got underway. The professional men's division has started their race. Reigning men’s champion John Korir of Kenya is back to defend his title. The entire men’s podium and seven of the top 10 finishers from last year are back, including runners with three of the top eight times in race history. The professional women will follow, in about 10 minutes. Today's race marks the 50th anniversary of the “Run for the Hoses,” when Jack Fultz won the Boston Marathon in temperatures approaching 100 degrees. Fortunately, cool weather greeted the runners in Hopkinton today and was expected to reach into the 40s. Fultz, who was serving as grand marshal, said as he waited to board his ride that the weather was the “polar opposite” from the day of his 1976 win. “I am just trying to soak it all in, to remember it all,” he said. “There are almost are no words to fully describe the kind of experience. You have a dream of a lifetime and all of a sudden it comes true.” The second of the elite races has started, with the women's wheelchair division crossing the starting line and beginning their trek to Boston. Defending women's wheelchair champion Susannah Scaroni is expecting a baby in August and not racing. Previous winners Manuela Schar of Switzerland, Tatyana McFadden of the United States and Eden Rainbow-Cooper of Britain are all in the field. The men's wheelchair division has officially taken off, kicking off the 2026 Boston Marathon. Eight-time wheelchair champion Marcel Hug of Switzerland is going for another victory, which would put him one short of Ernst Van Dyk's all-category record of 10. (Clarence DeMar won the open division seven times from 1911-30.) Hug will be chased by two-time winner Daniel Romanchuk of Champaign, Illinois. The Boston Athletic Association has been sharing some great pre-race images on their X account on Monday morning, including shots of some of the professional division participants getting ready for the race. Here's a closer look: Do you know someone running in this year's Boston Marathon? Or do you just want to see how celebrity runners like astronaut Suni Williams or "Love Island USA" winner Bryan Arenales are doing? You can track runners using the Boston Athletic Association Racing App, which is available in the App Store and on Google Play. It features live tracking, athlete leaderboards and more. Here's how to download it. Police officials held a safety briefing shortly after 8 a.m. ahead of the marathon getting underway in Hopkinton. Local, state and federal officials spoke about preparations for race day. "The priority of the FBI will always be the safety and security of the public," Ted Docks, special agent in charge at FBI Boston said. "There is no specific or credible threats targeting this year's race. However we are in a heightened threat environment." "We're not taking anything for granted," he added. Docks said federal law enforcement will be monitoring the event. Grace Taylor's dream of running the Boston Marathon is coming true, as she embarks on her first Boston Marathon run representing Mass General's Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer Program. The weather looks good, Sharon Lokedi is fit and the fastest field in Boston Marathon history could push her to a second straight course record — if she decides to go for it. A year after shattering the women’s mark by more than 2 1/2 minutes, the defending champion heads to the starting line in Hopkinton on Monday for the 130th edition of the world’s oldest and most prestigious annual marathon. Reigning men’s champion and fellow Kenyan John Korir also is back to lead a field of more than 30,000 on the 26.2-mile race to Boston’s Copley Square. Cool weather and an expected tailwind will greet them in Hopkinton — perhaps the ideal conditions for more fast times like last year, when Lokedi finished in 2 hours, 17 minutes, 22 seconds to break the 11-year-old course record and deprive runner-up Hellen Obiri of a third straight win. Korir's 2:04:45 was the third-fastest ever as he joined his brother to become a Boston Marathon champion. “Last year was crazy fast, so I don’t know if it will be the same thing this year. But whichever one, I’m excited for,” Lokedi said last week as she prepared to defend her title. “You never know. I feel like that is always determined by when you get to the start line.” It's the 130th running of the iconic race.It’s the 130th running of the iconic race. Marathon Monday in Boston is here, and tens of thousands of runners are set to make the legendary 26.2-mile trek from Hopkinton to Copley Square starting just after 9 a.m. This year is the 130th running of the iconic marathon, and more than 30,000 runners from over 130 countries and all 50 states will be tackling the course. It's a day like no other in Boston and seven other Massachusetts communities along the route — Hopkinton, Ashland, Framingham, Natick, Wellesley, Newton and Brookline. Here's the schedule for starting times: Read Full ArticleIt’ll feel like the low 40s today with the wind chill. Layer up if you’re heading out to watch the 130th Boston Marathon. It’s going to be chilly and breezy. The race starts in Hopkinton around 9 a.m., and temperatures will be the 30s. Runners will be “gifted” a tail wind for much of the 26.2-mile course toward downtown Boston. By the early afternoon, clouds develop, and there could be a few light showers across the region. For those cheering on the Boston Red Sox at Fenway Monday, you may also have to deal with some light rain at times, especially in the later innings. Highs on Patriots’ Day only reach the upper 40s, and it will feel like the low 40s all afternoon when you add in the wind. That’s about 10 degrees below average for this time of year. Watch for some frost Tuesday morning with temperatures in the low to mid 30s. Once again, highs will only be in the mid to upper 40s Tuesday afternoon.
